claim: TDP-43 is abundantly expressed by all Sox10-positive Schwann cells.
source: TDP-43 is abundantly expressed by all Sox10-positive Schwann cells (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B demonstrating TDP-43 expression in Sox10-positive Schwann cells.

claim: In TDP-43 conditional knockout mice, TDP-43 expression is completely abolished in Schwann cells.
source: In these conditional knockout (cKO) mice, TDP-43 expression is completely abolished in Schwann cells (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing absence of TDP-43 in Sox10-positive Schwann cells in cKO mice.

claim: Action potential propagation is delayed by approximately 50% in TDP-43 cKO mice at postnatal day 27.
source: By measuring the motor nerve conduction velocity, we find that action potential propagation is delayed by ~50% in the cKO mice at postnatal day (P) 27 (Figure 1A, C).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 1C demonstrating reduced conduction velocity in cKO mice.

claim: The cKO sciatic nerves appear normal in size and opacity compared to wild-type nerves.
source: However, the cKO sciatic nerves appear normal in size and opacity compared to wild-type (WT) nerves (Figure 1D), suggesting that compact myelin is being formed normally.
evidence: Supported by visual inspection shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A slight decrease in the number of myelinated axons is observed in the cKO nerves at P3.
source: While a slight decrease in the number of myelinated axons is observed in the cKO nerves at P3, they recover to control levels by P21 (Figure 1E, F)
evidence: Supported by quantification from electron microscopy shown in Figure 1E, F.

claim: The number of myelinated axons in cKO nerves recovers to control levels by P21.
source: While a slight decrease in the number of myelinated axons is observed in the cKO nerves at P3, they recover to control levels by P21 (Figure 1E, F)
evidence: Supported by quantification from electron microscopy shown in Figure 1E, F.

claim: Myelin thickness in cKO nerves is comparable to wild-type.
source: they recover to control levels by P21 (Figure 1E, F) with myelin thickness comparable to the WT (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by g-ratio analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Schwann cell TDP-43 is required for normal nerve conduction velocity despite normal appearance of compact myelin.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that Schwann cell TDP-43 is required for normal nerve conduction velocity, despite the normal appearance of compact myelin in the TDP-43-cKO mice.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of conduction delay data and normal myelin structure observations.

claim: Paranodal junctions serve as a multifunctional diffusion barrier required for maximal axon insulation provided by myelin sheaths.
source: Paranodal axoglial junctions serve as a multifunctional diffusion barrier that is required for maximal axon insulation provided by myelin sheaths (Pedraza et al., 2001; Rosenbluth, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Pedraza et al., 2001; Rosenbluth, 2009).

claim: Mouse mutants lacking paranodal junctions display an approximately 40-50% delay in nerve conduction without gross myelination defects.
source: Mouse mutants lacking paranodal junctions display an ~40–50% delay in nerve conduction without gross myelination defects (Bhat et al., 2001; Pillai et al., 2009; Susuki et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Bhat et al., 2001; Pillai et al., 2009; Susuki et al., 2013).

claim: Paranodal junctions comprise three key cell adhesion molecules: axonal Caspr, axonal contactin, and glial neurofascin 155 kDa isoform.
source: Paranodal junctions comprise three key cell adhesion molecules—axonal Caspr (contactin-associated protein), axonal contactin (Cntn), and glial neurofascin (NFasc) 155 kDa isoform (NF155), each of which is essential for paranodal junction formation (Poliak and Peles, 2003; Salzer, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Poliak and Peles, 2003; Salzer, 2003).

claim: In mature wild-type PNS, Nav channels and NF186 are enriched at nodes of Ranvier.
source: In the mature WT PNS, Nav channels and axonal 186 kDa isoform of NFasc (NF186) are enriched at nodes of Ranvier, whereas NF155 and Caspr/Cntn are highly clustered at paranodal domains flanking each node (Figure 2A, B [nodes indicated by open arrowheads and paranodes by solid arrowheads], Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A, B, C.

claim: In mature wild-type PNS, NF155 and Caspr/Cntn are highly clustered at paranodal domains flanking each node.
source: In the mature WT PNS, Nav channels and axonal 186 kDa isoform of NFasc (NF186) are enriched at nodes of Ranvier, whereas NF155 and Caspr/Cntn are highly clustered at paranodal domains flanking each node (Figure 2A, B [nodes indicated by open arrowheads and paranodes by solid arrowheads], Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A, B, C.

claim: Caspr clustering is no longer detected at paranodes in the TDP-43 cKO at P28.
source: In stark contrast to the WT and conditional heterozygote (cHet), the prototypical Caspr clustering is no longer detected at paranodes in the cKO at P28 (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cntn, NF155, and AnkB are not detected at paranodes in the TDP-43 cKO.
source: and neither are Cntn, NF155, and the NF155-associated scaffold protein AnkB (Chang et al., 2014; Figure 2B–D), indicating that paranodal junctions are disrupted in the TDP-43 cKO.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Paranodal junctions are disrupted in the TDP-43 cKO.
source: and neither are Cntn, NF155, and the NF155-associated scaffold protein AnkB (Chang et al., 2014; Figure 2B–D), indicating that paranodal junctions are disrupted in the TDP-43 cKO.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of paranodal junction components shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Caspr is absent at paranodes in P3 TDP-43 cKO sciatic nerves while gliomedin remains clustered at nascent nodes.
source: To determine whether paranodal junctions are not assembled during early development in the TDP-43 cKO or are initially formed but not stabilized during and after myelination, we examined P3 sciatic nerves (initiation of myelination) and found that Caspr is absent at paranodes while the Schwann cell-secreted extracellular matrix component gliomedin (Gldn) (Eshed et al., 2005) remains clustered at nascent nodes (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Paranodal junctions fail to form starting from the initiation of myelination in the absence of Schwann cell TDP-43.
source: This strongly suggests that paranodal junctions fail to form starting from the initiation of myelination in the absence of Schwann cell TDP-43.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Caspr is absent at paranodes at P3, the initiation of myelination.

claim: One hallmark alteration of losing the diffusion barrier function exerted by paranodal junctions is translocation of Kv1 channels from juxtaparanodal regions to paranodes.
source: One hallmark alteration of losing the diffusion barrier function exerted by paranodal junctions is translocation of the Shaker-type voltage-gated potassium (Kv1) channels and their associated protein complex from juxtaparanodal regions to paranodes (Poliak and Peles, 2003; Salzer, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Poliak and Peles, 2003; Salzer, 2003).

claim: In wild-type nerves, Kv1.1 and Kv1.2 channels and Caspr2 are concentrated in the juxtaparanodal domains and separated from nodes of Ranvier by paranodal junctions.
source: In WT nerves, Kv1.1 and Kv1.2 channels and Caspr2 are concentrated in the juxtaparanodal domains and separated from nodes of Ranvier by paranodal junctions (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: In the TDP-43 cKO sciatic nerves, Kv1.1, Kv1.2, and Caspr2 invade the paranodes.
source: Strikingly, in the cKO sciatic nerves these components invade the paranodes (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: The paranodal loops in the TDP-43 cKO detach from the axons ultrastructurally.
source: Ultrastructurally, the paranodal loops in the cKO detach from the axons. The loops are no longer tightly apposed to the axon, resulting in the absence of the clear indentation of the axolemma, typically observed in WT nerves (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Schwann cell TDP-43 plays a cell-autonomous role in assembling paranodal junctions and establishing polarized molecular domains at nodes of Ranvier.
source: Taken together, our findings strongly suggest a cell-autonomous role of Schwann cell TDP-43 in assembling paranodal junctions and properly establishing the polarized molecular domains at nodes of Ranvier.
evidence: Inferred from the multiple observations of paranodal junction disruption in TDP-43 cKO.

claim: Mutant mice lacking paranodal junctions in both PNS and CNS exhibit tremors, paralysis, and ataxia.
source: Mutant mice lacking paranodal junctions in both the PNS and CNS exhibit tremors, paralysis, and ataxia (Berglund et al., 1999; Bhat et al., 2001; Coetzee et al., 1996; Pillai et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Berglund et al., 1999; Bhat et al., 2001; Coetzee et al., 1996; Pillai et al., 2009).

claim: TDP-43 cKO mice do not exhibit a gross neurological deficit when observed in their home cage.
source: Despite the lack of paranodal junctions in the PNS, the TDP-43-cKO mice (by Dhh-Cre or Mpz-Cre) do not exhibit a gross neurological deficit when observed in their home cage.
evidence: Based on observational assessment of mice in home cage.

claim: TDP-43 cKO mice perform significantly worse than wild-type littermates on the rotarod test.
source: However, when challenged with the rotarod test, the cKO mice perform significantly worse than WT littermates (Figure 2H), suggesting that PNS paranodal junctions are required for optimal motor performance.
evidence: Supported by rotarod test data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: PNS paranodal junctions are required for optimal motor performance.
source: However, when challenged with the rotarod test, the cKO mice perform significantly worse than WT littermates (Figure 2H), suggesting that PNS paranodal junctions are required for optimal motor performance.
evidence: Inferred from the motor performance deficit in TDP-43 cKO mice lacking paranodal junctions.

claim: Paranodal junction assembly in both PNS and CNS requires Caspr, Cntn, and NF155.
source: Given that paranodal junction assembly in both the PNS and CNS requires Caspr, Cntn, and NF155 (Poliak and Peles, 2003; Salzer, 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Poliak and Peles, 2003; Salzer, 2003).

claim: Caspr clusters are clearly detected in the TDP-43 cKO spinal cords.
source: Surprisingly, Caspr clusters are still clearly detected in the cKO spinal cords (Figure 3A, B), indicating that TDP-43 is dispensable for CNS paranodal junction formation.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: TDP-43 is dispensable for CNS paranodal junction formation.
source: Surprisingly, Caspr clusters are still clearly detected in the cKO spinal cords (Figure 3A, B), indicating that TDP-43 is dispensable for CNS paranodal junction formation.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of Caspr clusters in TDP-43 cKO spinal cords.

claim: At the dorsal root transition zone, paranodal junctions fail to form exclusively on the PNS side in the TDP-43 cKO and not on the CNS side.
source: The dramatic difference in the requirement for TDP-43 between the PNS and CNS is highlighted at the dorsal root transition zone, where the paranodal junctions fail to form exclusively on the PNS side in the cKO and not on the CNS side (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cajal bands are clearly visible in TDP-43 cKO nerves.
source: We examined the nerves for βII spectrin (Susuki et al., 2011) and found that Cajal bands are clearly visible in the absence of TDP-43 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The juxtamesaxon is formed normally in the absence of TDP-43.
source: In the absence of TDP-43, the juxtamesaxon is formed normally (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Tight, gap, and adherens junction components (ZO-1, Cx32, and E-cadherin) are normally enriched at paranodes in the TDP-43 cKO.
source: By immunostaining for the junctional components (zonula occludens-1 [ZO-1], connexin 32 [Cx32], and E-cadherin [E-cad], respectively), we find that they are all normally enriched at paranodes in the cKO (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: Schmidt-Lanterman incisures are normally formed in the TDP-43 cKO.
source: Lastly, Schmidt–Lanterman incisures, the cytoplasmic channels that run through the compact myelin and connect the outermost and innermost cytoplasmic compartments of Schwann cells, can be identified by staining for myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG). Once again, the incisures were normally formed, as observed by the classic funnel-shaped MAG staining in the TDP-43 cKO (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The major effect of ablating TDP-43 in Schwann cells specifically lies in the disruption of paranodal junctions.
source: Taken together, by examining the fine structures found in Schwann cell myelin, our findings suggest that the major effect of ablating TDP-43 in Schwann cells specifically lies in the disruption of paranodal junctions.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that other Schwann cell structures remain intact while paranodal junctions are disrupted.

claim: Among the essential paranodal junction components, only NF155 is expressed by Schwann cells.
source: Among the known essential components, Caspr/Cntn and NF155, only NF155 is expressed by Schwann cells.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cell-type specific expression patterns.

claim: NFasc staining is absent from the paranodes in the TDP-43 cKO.
source: Consistent with disrupted expression of NF155, not only is NFasc staining absent from the paranodes in the TDP-43 cKO (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), but NFasc is also undetectable at the incisures (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Figure 4F.

claim: NFasc is undetectable at the incisures in the TDP-43 cKO.
source: Consistent with disrupted expression of NF155, not only is NFasc staining absent from the paranodes in the TDP-43 cKO (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), but NFasc is also undetectable at the incisures (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In mice lacking Caspr or galactocerebroside/sulfatide, NF155 remains localized at the incisures although not highly clustered at paranodes.
source: By contrast, although NF155 is not highly clustered at the paranodes in mice lacking Caspr or galactocerebroside/sulfatide, it remains localized at the incisures (Poliak et al., 2001; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citation to Poliak et al., 2001.

claim: NF155 expression is abolished in the absence of TDP-43.
source: Taken together, these data strongly suggest that NF155 expression is abolished in the absence of TDP-43.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of NFasc at both paranodes and incisures in TDP-43 cKO.

claim: Alternative splicing of Nfasc generates NFasc proteins with different domain architectures in different cell types.
source: Alternative splicing generates NFasc proteins with different domain architectures of the extracellular moiety in different cell types (Davis et al., 1996; Davis et al., 1993; Tait et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Davis et al., 1996; Davis et al., 1993; Tait et al., 2000).

claim: In Schwann cells, Nfasc mRNA contains exons 23 and 24 while exons 28-30 are excluded, producing the glial-specific NF155 isoform.
source: In Schwann cells, Nfasc mRNA contains exons 23 and 24 while exons 28–30 are excluded, producing the glial-specific NF155 isoform.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Nfasc alternative splicing patterns.

claim: In neurons, Nfasc transcripts are spliced in the opposite way and are translated into the neuronal-specific NF186 isoform.
source: In neurons, Nfasc transcripts are spliced in the opposite way and are translated into the neuronal-specific NF186 isoform.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Nfasc alternative splicing patterns.

claim: NF155 is undetectable in the TDP-43 cKO sciatic nerves by western blotting.
source: When the expression of NFasc proteins in sciatic nerves is analyzed by western blotting, we find that NF155 is undetectable in the TDP-43 cKO whereas the level of NF186 is unchanged (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The level of NF186 is unchanged in the TDP-43 cKO sciatic nerves.
source: When the expression of NFasc proteins in sciatic nerves is analyzed by western blotting, we find that NF155 is undetectable in the TDP-43 cKO whereas the level of NF186 is unchanged (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The protein expression of Caspr in the TDP-43 cKO nerve remains unchanged.
source: Similarly, the protein expression of Caspr in the cKO nerve also remains unchanged (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: NFasc is already absent from the TDP-43 cKO paranodes at P3.
source: Moreover, by immunostaining the nascent nodes and paranodes in P3 sciatic nerves, NFasc is already absent from the cKO paranodes (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The mRNA for NF155 is dramatically decreased in the TDP-43 cKO.
source: Consistently, the mRNA for NF155 is dramatically decreased in the cKO (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Ablating TDP-43 in Schwann cells leads to aberrant NF155 expression resulting in failure of Caspr to cluster at paranodes and form paranodal junctions.
source: Therefore, our findings strongly suggest that ablating TDP-43 in Schwann cells leads to aberrant NF155 expression and in turn results in the failure of Caspr to cluster at paranodes and form paranodal junctions.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of reduced NF155 expression and absence of paranodal junctions in TDP-43 cKO.

claim: TDP-43 binds to more than 6000 RNA targets in the brain.
source: TDP-43 binds to more than 6000 RNA targets in the brain (Polymenidou et al., 2011; Tollervey et al., 2011)—roughly 30% of the total transcriptome
evidence: Supported by citations to previous CLIP-seq studies (Polymenidou et al., 2011; Tollervey et al., 2011).

claim: TDP-43 binds to roughly 30% of the total transcriptome in the brain.
source: TDP-43 binds to more than 6000 RNA targets in the brain (Polymenidou et al., 2011; Tollervey et al., 2011)—roughly 30% of the total transcriptome
evidence: Supported by citations to previous CLIP-seq studies (Polymenidou et al., 2011; Tollervey et al., 2011).

claim: Intron 17 of Nfasc contains a UG-rich sequence, a known consensus RNA-binding motif for TDP-43.
source: Because intron 17 contains a UG-rich sequence, a known consensus RNA-binding motif for TDP-43 (Polymenidou et al., 2011; Tollervey et al., 2011; Figure 6A, B)
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6A, B and citations to previous literature (Polymenidou et al., 2011; Tollervey et al., 2011).

claim: A single cluster of pre-mRNA binding peaks for TDP-43 on Nfasc is located at intron 17.
source: we data-mined the previously published cross-linking immunoprecipitation and high-throughput sequencing (CLIP-seq) data on TDP-43-binding transcripts in mouse brains (Polymenidou et al., 2011) and identify a single cluster of pre-mRNA binding peaks on Nfasc located at intron 17 (upper panel of Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by analysis of published CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A 104-bp-long cassette exon exists in the TDP-43 cKO with a well-defined splice acceptor and splice donor, just upstream to the TDP-43-binding peaks.
source: Further analysis reveals a 104-bp-long cassette exon in the cKO with a well-defined splice acceptor and splice donor, just upstream to the TDP-43-binding peaks (Figure 6B), characteristic of TDP-43-repressed cryptic exons (Ling et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6B and citation to Ling et al., 2015.

claim: The cryptic exon in Nfasc is characteristic of TDP-43-repressed cryptic exons.
source: Further analysis reveals a 104-bp-long cassette exon in the cKO with a well-defined splice acceptor and splice donor, just upstream to the TDP-43-binding peaks (Figure 6B), characteristic of TDP-43-repressed cryptic exons (Ling et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature on TDP-43-repressed cryptic exons (Ling et al., 2015).

claim: There is near complete utilization (93.1%) of the cryptic exon splice acceptor in the TDP-43 cKO sciatic nerves compared with 25.3% in wild-type nerves.
source: Quantitative splice junction analyses using the percent spliced in index (PSI) reveal a near complete utilization of the cryptic exon splice acceptor (93.1%) in the cKO sciatic nerves compared with 25.3% in the WT nerves (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by PSI analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The usage of the cryptic splice acceptor is less dramatic (43.9%) in the spinal cords from TDP-43 cKO mice.
source: By contrast, the usage of this cryptic splice acceptor is less dramatic (43.9%) in the spinal cords from the same TDP-43-cKO mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by PSI analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cryptic exon region contains a premature stop codon when spliced with the upstream constitutive exon 17.
source: More critically, this newly identified cryptic exon region contains a premature stop codon when spliced with the upstream constitutive exon 17 (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A premature stop codon is the trigger for nonsense-mediated decay.
source: A premature stop codon is the trigger for nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) (Karousis and Mühlemann, 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Karousis and Mühlemann, 2019).

claim: The premature stop codon provides the mechanistic explanation for the dramatic reduction of Nfasc transcripts and absence of NFasc protein in TDP-43-deleted Schwann cells.
source: A premature stop codon is the trigger for nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) (Karousis and Mühlemann, 2019), thereby providing the mechanistic explanation to the dramatic reduction of Nfasc transcripts and the absence of NFasc protein in the TDP-43-deleted Schwann cells (Figure 4F, Figure 5).
evidence: Inferred from the presence of premature stop codon and knowledge of NMD mechanism.

claim: A discrete band representing a potential truncated NFasc protein is undetectable in the TDP-43 cKO by western blotting.
source: A discrete band representing a potential truncated NFasc protein (with calculated molecular weight of 69 kDa before glycosylation, caused by the premature stop codon) is undetectable in the cKO by western blotting (Figure 5B)
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The remaining 20% of Nfasc transcripts in the TDP-43 cKO could be en route for degradation.
source: suggesting that the remaining 20% transcripts could be en route for degradation.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the absence of truncated protein despite presence of some transcripts.

claim: The predominant Nfasc isoform uses exons 17 and 19 and excludes exon 18 in wild-type and cHet mice.
source: The predominant Nfasc isoform uses exons 17 and 19 and excludes exon 18 in the WT and cHet mice (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The predominant Nfasc isoform uses CE1 in the TDP-43 cKO sciatic nerves.
source: Consistent with the bioinformatic analysis, the predominant Nfasc isoform uses CE1 in the cKO sciatic nerves (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The utilization of CE1 is not observed in the majority of Nfasc transcripts in the spinal cords from TDP-43 cKO mice.
source: By contrast, the utilization of CE1 is not observed in the majority of Nfasc transcripts in the spinal cords from the same TDP-43-cKO mice, and the CE1-containing PCR product is only faintly detected.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data described in the text.

claim: TDP-43 is required for proper splicing of the vast majority of Nfasc transcripts in Schwann cells, but not oligodendrocytes.
source: Taken together, the data indicate an increased usage of the cryptic exon in Nfasc upon the loss of TDP-43 in the myelinating glia, where TDP-43 is required for proper splicing of the vast majority of Nfasc transcripts in Schwann cells, but not oligodendrocytes.
evidence: Inferred from the differential cryptic exon usage in PNS versus CNS in TDP-43 cKO.

claim: Gene expression profiles change dramatically when Schwann cells transition from actively myelinating to the mature state.
source: Gene expression profiles change dramatically when Schwann cells transition from actively myelinating to the mature state (Patzig et al., 2011; Siems et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Patzig et al., 2011; Siems et al., 2020).

claim: Paranodal junctions are still absent in P60 TDP-43 cKO nerves.
source: It is clear from the analysis of the P60 cKO nerves that paranodal junctions are still absent (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E, Figure 3A), suggesting a lack of compensatory factors in the mature state that may bypass the need for TDP-43.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E and Figure 3A.

claim: There is a lack of compensatory factors in the mature state that may bypass the need for TDP-43 in Schwann cells.
source: It is clear from the analysis of the P60 cKO nerves that paranodal junctions are still absent (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E, Figure 3A), suggesting a lack of compensatory factors in the mature state that may bypass the need for TDP-43.
evidence: Inferred from the persistent absence of paranodal junctions in mature TDP-43 cKO nerves.

claim: At 3 months post-tamoxifen injection, NFasc is absent from a similar proportion of Schmidt-Lanterman incisures in the sciatic nerves and ventral roots of TDP-43 icKO mice.
source: At 3 months post-tamoxifen injection, NFasc is absent from a similar proportion of Schmidt–Lanterman incisures in the sciatic nerves and ventral roots (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RT-PCR analysis of TDP-43 icKO sciatic nerves reveals a dramatic increase in CE1 usage of Nfasc transcripts.
source: RT-PCR analysis of the sciatic nerves reveals a dramatic increase in the CE1 usage of Nfasc transcripts (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: TDP-43 continues to play an essential role in regulating NFasc expression by repressing CE inclusion even in the mature state.
source: These observations suggest that TDP-43 continues to play an essential role in regulating NFasc expression by repressing the CE inclusion even in the mature state.
evidence: Inferred from the increased CE1 usage and loss of NFasc in mature Schwann cells after TDP-43 deletion.

claim: NFasc is notorious for its stability in molecular domains and requires a long time for protein turnover after adult or juvenile NFasc deletion.
source: NFasc is notorious for its stability in the molecular domains where it is involved and requires a long time for protein turnover after adult or juvenile NFasc deletion (8–16 weeks at nodes; ≥8 weeks at paranodes) (Desmazieres et al., 2014; Pillai et al., 2009; Zonta et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Desmazieres et al., 2014; Pillai et al., 2009; Zonta et al., 2011).

claim: The paranodal diffusion barrier is compromised in TDP-43 icKO nerves.
source: While NFasc protein is absent from the TDP-43-icKO incisures with residual NFasc still detected at paranodes to different extent, the paranodal diffusion barrier is compromised (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Paranodal diffusion barrier compromise in TDP-43 icKO ranges from paranodal invasion of Kv1.1 to fragmentation or shortening of Caspr clusters.
source: This ranges from paranodal invasion of Kv1.1 to fragmentation or shortening of Caspr clusters (Figure 7C), and is consistent with the ongoing disassembly of paranodal junctions, similar to when Nfasc is ablated from mature Schwann cells (Pillai et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7C and citation to Pillai et al., 2009.

claim: The proportion of paranodal junctions that are disrupted at 5 months post-tamoxifen injection is similar to the icKO recombination efficiency.
source: The proportion of paranodal junctions that are disrupted at 5 months post-tamoxifen injection is similar to the icKO recombination efficiency (Figure 7D), suggesting that paranodal disruption is prevalent among the mature Schwann cells lacking TDP-43.
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Paranodal disruption is prevalent among mature Schwann cells lacking TDP-43.
source: The proportion of paranodal junctions that are disrupted at 5 months post-tamoxifen injection is similar to the icKO recombination efficiency (Figure 7D), suggesting that paranodal disruption is prevalent among the mature Schwann cells lacking TDP-43.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between recombination efficiency and paranodal disruption.

claim: TDP-43 in mature Schwann cells continues to repress CE inclusion and supply NFasc for maintaining paranodal junctions.
source: Altogether, our findings strongly suggest that TDP-43 in mature Schwann cells continues to repress the CE inclusion and supply NFasc for maintaining paranodal junctions.
evidence: Inferred from the observations in the inducible knockout experiments.

claim: Deletion of TDP-43 in Schwann cells results in a dramatic delay in peripheral nerve conduction causing significant motor deficits in mice.
source: We demonstrate that deletion of TDP-43 in Schwann cells results in a dramatic delay in peripheral nerve conduction causing significant motor deficits in mice, which is directly attributed to the absence of paranodal axoglial junctions.
evidence: Supported by conduction velocity measurements and rotarod test data.

claim: The conduction delay in TDP-43 cKO mice is directly attributed to the absence of paranodal axoglial junctions.
source: We demonstrate that deletion of TDP-43 in Schwann cells results in a dramatic delay in peripheral nerve conduction causing significant motor deficits in mice, which is directly attributed to the absence of paranodal axoglial junctions.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between paranodal junction loss and conduction delay.

claim: Paranodes in the central nervous system are unaltered in oligodendrocytes lacking TDP-43.
source: By contrast, paranodes in the central nervous system are unaltered in oligodendrocytes lacking TDP-43.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing intact Caspr clusters in CNS.

claim: TDP-43 binds directly to Neurofascin mRNA.
source: Mechanistically, TDP-43 binds directly to Neurofascin mRNA, encoding the cell adhesion molecule essential for paranode assembly and maintenance.
evidence: Supported by CLIP-seq data showing TDP-43 binding peaks on Nfasc.

claim: Loss of TDP-43 triggers the retention of a previously unidentified cryptic exon in Neurofascin mRNA.
source: Loss of TDP-43 triggers the retention of a previously unidentified cryptic exon, which targets Neurofascin mRNA for nonsense-mediated decay.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and RT-PCR data showing cryptic exon inclusion in TDP-43 cKO.

claim: The cryptic exon in Neurofascin mRNA targets the transcript for nonsense-mediated decay.
source: Loss of TDP-43 triggers the retention of a previously unidentified cryptic exon, which targets Neurofascin mRNA for nonsense-mediated decay.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of premature stop codon in the cryptic exon and knowledge of NMD mechanism.

claim: TDP-43 is required for neurofascin expression, proper assembly and maintenance of paranodes, and rapid saltatory conduction.
source: Thus, TDP-43 is required for neurofascin expression, proper assembly and maintenance of paranodes, and rapid saltatory conduction.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of NFasc loss, paranodal disruption, and conduction delay in TDP-43 cKO.

claim: TDP-43 modulates target gene expression by regulating mRNA stability, splicing, polyadenylation site selection, transport, and translation.
source: TDP-43 binds to more than 6000 RNA targets in the brain (Polymenidou et al., 2011; Tollervey et al., 2011)—roughly 30% of the total transcriptome—and modulates target gene expression by regulating mRNA stability, splicing, polyadenylation site selection, transport, and translation (Ederle and Dormann, 2017; Ling et al., 2013; Rot et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Ederle and Dormann, 2017; Ling et al., 2013; Rot et al., 2017).

claim: TDP-43-containing pathological aggregates have been detected in numerous neurodegenerative diseases including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia.
source: The detection of TDP-43-containing pathological aggregates in numerous neurodegenerative diseases—including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia—has resulted in the classification of a spectrum of disorders known as TDP-43 proteinopathies (Kwong et al., 2008; Ling et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Kwong et al., 2008; Ling et al., 2013).

claim: Both loss of function and gain of toxic properties may contribute to the neurodegeneration associated with TDP-43 proteinopathies.
source: It is widely considered that both loss of function and gain of toxic properties may contribute to the neurodegeneration associated with TDP-43 proteinopathies (Ling et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Ling et al., 2013).

claim: The cells of the peripheral nervous system are affected in ALS patients with differential vulnerability.
source: Intriguingly, it is known that the cells of the peripheral nervous system (PNS) are also affected in ALS patients with differential vulnerability (Gentile et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Gentile et al., 2019).

claim: Schwann cells ensheathe and myelinate all relevant axons of the peripheral nerves.
source: Schwann cells ensheathe and myelinate all relevant axons of the peripheral nerves (Nave and Werner, 2014; Salzer, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Nave and Werner, 2014; Salzer, 2015).

claim: Schwann cell-axon interactions highly cluster voltage-gated sodium channels at nodes of Ranvier, enabling rapid saltatory conduction.
source: Moreover, Schwann cell–axon interactions highly cluster voltage-gated sodium (Nav) channels at nodes of Ranvier, thus enabling rapid saltatory conduction (Poliak and Peles, 2003; Salzer, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Poliak and Peles, 2003; Salzer, 2003).

claim: Paranodal axoglial junctions are essential for the maximal insulatory function of myelin.
source: The intricate interactions between axons and Schwann cells further establish the paranodal axoglial junctions that flank nodes of Ranvier and are essential for the maximal insulatory function of myelin (Pedraza et al., 2001; Rosenbluth, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Pedraza et al., 2001; Rosenbluth, 2009).

claim: TDP-43 cKO mice display a 50% delay in nerve conduction with motor deficits, without any apparent structural alteration in compact myelin.
source: In mice lacking TDP-43 in Schwann cells, we find a 50% delay in nerve conduction with motor deficits, without any apparent structural alteration in compact myelin.
evidence: Supported by conduction velocity measurements, rotarod tests, and electron microscopy data.

claim: The deficit in paranodal junctions is exclusive to Schwann cells and not observed in oligodendrocyte paranodes in the central nervous system.
source: This deficit is exclusive to Schwann cells and not observed in oligodendrocyte paranodes in the central nervous system (CNS).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing intact CNS paranodes but disrupted PNS paranodes.

claim: TDP-43 is required for the expression of Neurofascin by repressing the usage of a cryptic exon during splicing.
source: Furthermore, we find that TDP-43 is required for the expression of Neurofascin (Nfasc), which encodes a glial cell adhesion molecule necessary for paranodal junction formation and maintenance, by repressing the usage of a cryptic exon during splicing.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq, RT-PCR, and western blot data showing cryptic exon inclusion and loss of NFasc in TDP-43 cKO.

claim: Loss of function for TDP-43 in Schwann cells results in impaired conduction velocity and motor behavior.
source: Our findings are the first demonstration of a functional role for TDP-43 in axon–glial interactions in the PNS and that the loss of function for TDP-43 in Schwann cells results in impaired conduction velocity and motor behavior.
evidence: Supported by conduction velocity measurements and rotarod test data.

claim: The myelinated axons in the TDP-43 cKO tend to have smaller diameters.
source: The possession of a myriad of targets implies that TDP-43 is a pleiotropic gene, and we find that the myelinated axons in the TDP-43 cKO tend to have smaller diameters that may also contribute to the conduction delay (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by axon diameter distribution data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The absence of paranodal junctions in mice lacking Caspr or Schwann cell NFasc results in approximately 40-50% peripheral nerve conduction delay.
source: However, from various studies, the absence of paranodal junctions in mice lacking Caspr or Schwann cell NFasc results in ~40–50% peripheral nerve conduction delay (Bhat et al., 2001; Pillai et al., 2009; Susuki et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Bhat et al., 2001; Pillai et al., 2009; Susuki et al., 2013).

claim: An average 52% delay in nerve conduction is observed in the TDP-43 cKO.
source: and we observe an average 52% delay in the TDP-43 cKO, suggesting that the absence of Schwann cell NFasc and paranodal junctions is the main contributor to the conduction delay in the TDP-43 cKO.
evidence: Supported by conduction velocity measurements.

claim: The absence of Schwann cell NFasc and paranodal junctions is the main contributor to the conduction delay in the TDP-43 cKO.
source: and we observe an average 52% delay in the TDP-43 cKO, suggesting that the absence of Schwann cell NFasc and paranodal junctions is the main contributor to the conduction delay in the TDP-43 cKO.
evidence: Inferred from the similarity between the conduction delay in TDP-43 cKO and other paranodal junction mutants.

claim: Schwann cell differentiation and myelination are controlled under a network of interacting transcription factors and signaling pathways.
source: Schwann cell differentiation and myelination are controlled under a network of interacting transcription factors and signaling pathways (Monk et al., 2015; Stolt and Wegner, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Monk et al., 2015; Stolt and Wegner, 2016).

claim: Nfasc and Gldn mRNA expression in Schwann cells coincides with the onset of myelination.
source: Nfasc and Gldn mRNA expression in Schwann cells coincides with the onset of myelination (Basak et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Basak et al., 2007).

claim: Transcriptional control for myelination participates in orchestrating the formation of nodal and paranodal molecular domains during myelination.
source: Nfasc and Gldn mRNA expression in Schwann cells coincides with the onset of myelination (Basak et al., 2007), suggesting that the transcriptional control for myelination also participates in orchestrating the formation of nodal and paranodal molecular domains during myelination.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal correlation between myelination and nodal/paranodal gene expression.

claim: Transcriptional regulation alone is insufficient for controlling the precise timing of node assembly.
source: Nevertheless, the insufficiency of transcriptional regulation alone for controlling the precise timing of node assembly has recently been revealed for Gldn, whose node-inducing activity in premyelinating ensheathing Schwann cells is inhibited by Tolloid-like proteinases (Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020).

claim: The expression of TDP-43 is highly regulated during development.
source: Our identification of the novel cryptic exon residing in intron 17 of Nfasc may provide a fine-tuning mechanism governed by TDP-43, especially as the expression of TDP-43 is found to be highly regulated during development (Sephton et al., 2010) and may differ between cell types.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Sephton et al., 2010).

claim: The cryptic exon in Nfasc may provide a fine-tuning mechanism for NFasc expression governed by TDP-43.
source: Our identification of the novel cryptic exon residing in intron 17 of Nfasc may provide a fine-tuning mechanism governed by TDP-43, especially as the expression of TDP-43 is found to be highly regulated during development (Sephton et al., 2010) and may differ between cell types.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the discovery of the cryptic exon and knowledge of TDP-43 regulation.

claim: TDP-43 and NFasc are expressed by both Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes.
source: TDP-43 and NFasc are expressed by both Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes.
evidence: Based on established knowledge and immunostaining data.

claim: There is an increased usage of the Nfasc cryptic exon in the TDP-43 cKO spinal cords, although not to the same extent as in sciatic nerves.
source: Through our RNA-seq and splicing analyses, we also identify an increased usage of this Nfasc cryptic exon in the TDP-43-cKO spinal cords, although this usage is not increased to the same extent as in sciatic nerves.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and PSI analysis.

claim: TDP-43 performs in a similar manner on Nfasc expression by repressing the cryptic exon in both PNS and CNS myelinating glia.
source: This suggests that TDP-43 actually performs in a similar manner on Nfasc expression by repressing this cryptic exon in both PNS and CNS myelinating glia.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of cryptic exon usage in both PNS and CNS, albeit to different extents.

claim: The difference in the extent of Nfasc regulation in Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes may result from different compositions of RNA-binding proteins that regulate pre-mRNA splicing in different cell types.
source: Conceivably, the difference in the extent of regulation in Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes may result from the different compositions of various RNA-binding proteins that regulate pre-mRNA splicing in different cell types (Fu and Ares, 2014).
evidence: Speculative inference based on known cell-type differences in RNA-binding protein composition, supported by citation (Fu and Ares, 2014).

claim: Neuronal NFasc (NF186) is highly enriched at the axon initial segments and nodes and is required for maintaining the high density of Nav channels.
source: Furthermore, neuronal NFasc (NF186) is highly enriched at the axon initial segments and nodes and is required for maintaining the high density of Nav channels therein (Amor et al., 2017; Desmazieres et al., 2014; Zonta et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Amor et al., 2017; Desmazieres et al., 2014; Zonta et al., 2011).

claim: Ablation of neuronal NFasc drastically impairs the spontaneous firing of Purkinje neurons and delays peripheral nerve conduction.
source: Ablation of neuronal NFasc drastically impairs the spontaneous firing of Purkinje neurons and delays peripheral nerve conduction.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The newly identified Nfasc cryptic exon is located immediately downstream of a constitutive exon shared by all NFasc isoforms.
source: Given that this newly identified Nfasc cryptic exon is located immediately downstream of a constitutive exon shared by all NFasc isoforms
evidence: Based on sequence analysis of the Nfasc gene structure.

claim: Nfasc is among the top-21 downregulated genes when TDP-43 is overexpressed under the Thy1.2 promoter to induce its aggregation in neurons.
source: Although not discussed in a previous study where TDP-43 is overexpressed under the Thy1.2 promoter to induce its aggregation in neurons, Nfasc is among the top-21 downregulated genes (Shan et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Shan et al., 2010).

claim: TDP-43 aggregates have been described in both neurons and glia in the CNS for over a decade.
source: TDP-43 aggregates have been described in both neurons and glia in the CNS for over a decade (Arai et al., 2006; Neumann et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Arai et al., 2006; Neumann et al., 2006).

claim: Pathological TDP-43 aggregates were discovered in Schwann cells in an ALS patient.
source: It was not until recently that the pathological TDP-43 aggregates were discovered in Schwann cells in an ALS patient (Nakamura-Shindo et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Nakamura-Shindo et al., 2020).

claim: Optimal nerve conduction in the PNS provided by Schwann cell TDP-43 and paranodal junctions is essential for motor coordination.
source: Our findings reveal that Schwann cell TDP-43 is essential for the formation and maintenance of paranodal junctions, and the cKO mice display motor deficits when challenged on the rotarod, suggesting that optimal nerve conduction in the PNS provided by Schwann cell TDP-43 and paranodal junctions is essential for motor coordination.
evidence: Inferred from the motor deficits observed in TDP-43 cKO mice.
